result:
I want to write about small, ordinary miracles.

Not the kind with thunder, parting seas, or choirs of angels. I mean the kind that hide inside daily life so well that we usually mistake for nothing.

For example: the moment when a stranger laughs at something you say, and for one second the world becomes less cold. Or the way sunlight falls through a window in the late afternoon and turns a plain room into something golden, as if the universe decided to redecorate for ten minutes just for you. Or the instant when a song you haven’t heard in years comes on, and suddenly you are standing in another version of your life, wearing different clothes, carrying different worries, being someone you almost forgot you used to be.

There is a miracle in the fact that you can read these words at all. Symbols on a screen become sound in the mind, then meaning, then maybe feeling. Somewhere inside your brain, electricity and memory are collaborating to turn nothing more than shapes into a thought. And yet most of the time we don’t stop to be astonished by it. We are too busy wondering whether we remembered to reply to that message, or whether we should have said something different three years ago, or what to eat for dinner.

I like thinking about how much invisible work goes into being alive. The heart beating without being asked. The lungs doing their patient, rhythmic labor. The immune system fighting quiet battles. The brain assembling a coherent world from fragments of light and pressure and sound. All of it happening beneath awareness, like a vast city operating underneath a single lit window.

And then there are the emotional miracles, which are even stranger.

A person can break your heart, and somehow, after enough time, the heart repairs itself. Not exactly as it was, maybe. There are scars. There are new shapes. But it still loves again. That seems impossible until it happens.

Someone can say a single sentence to you at the right moment—“I believe in you,” “You are not alone,” “I’m sorry,” “Come home,” “Try again”—and that sentence can change the direction of a life. Words are so light in the mouth, yet they can be heavy enough to anchor a person to the world.

There is also the miracle of noticing.

Most days pass in a blur of tasks and screens and mild urgency. But occasionally, for no obvious reason, you become fully awake inside a moment. You notice the sound of rain on the roof. You notice the particular green of leaves after a storm. You notice the way someone’s face changes when they talk about something they love. You notice your own breath. You notice that you are here, at all, in this improbable body, on this improbable planet, moving through this improbable time.

Those moments don’t last. Maybe they aren’t meant to. If we were constantly aware of how extraordinary everything is, we might never be able to function. We might stand in the grocery store weeping over apples. We might miss appointments because we were too busy marveling at the fact that hands exist. We might forget to answer emails because we had become completely absorbed in the mystery of shadows on a wall.

Still, I think it is good to look for these small miracles. Not because they solve everything. They don’t. Life remains difficult, unfair, confusing, and full of loss. But noticing them is like lighting matches in a dark room. Each one is brief, and none of them replaces the sun. Yet together they make it possible to see.

Maybe that is why art matters so much. A poem, a song, a painting, a story—these are attempts to say: look, this too exists. This feeling you thought was only yours. This strange, tender, embarrassing, hopeful thing. Art reminds us that inner life is not private in the way we imagine. Other people have also stood awake at 3 a.m. wondering what they are doing. Other people have also loved too much, feared too much, wanted too much. Other people have also looked at the sky and felt both tiny and enormous at the same time.

I like the idea that every person carries an entire world inside them. From the outside, someone may be just another face on the street, another voice in a meeting, another name on a screen. But inside, there are cities. There are old wounds, secret jokes, favorite colors, memories that still sting, songs that still heal. There are rooms of the mind that haven’t been opened in years. There are doors we are afraid to walk through and windows we keep pretending not to see.

And sometimes, if we are lucky, someone opens one of those doors and says, “Oh, I know this place.”

That is connection. That is the miracle of being understood.

I also like the way ordinary objects become sacred through time. A mug with a chip in the rim. A jacket worn soft at the elbows. A book with a bent spine and pencil marks in the margins. A photograph faded by light. A key that no longer opens anything but is kept anyway. These things are not valuable because they are beautiful or rare. They are valuable because they have witnessed us. They have been near us while we lived. They have absorbed something of our days.

Perhaps that is why people keep things long after their usefulness is gone. We are not just keeping objects. We are keeping proof that certain moments happened. That we were there. That someone made us coffee once, or that we wore that coat on a winter walk when the air hurt our lungs, or that we wrote a sentence in a notebook when we were trying to become brave.

There is a miracle in continuation, too.

You wake up. You make tea, or coffee, or nothing. You open the curtains. You answer the messages. You step outside. The street is wet. The sky is pale. Someone walks a dog. A bus sighs to a stop. Life continues, not because it is easy, but because it has momentum. And within that momentum there are tiny openings: a moment to be kind, a moment to create, a moment to forgive, a moment to begin again.

I think people underestimate beginnings. We imagine them as dramatic: the first day of a new life, the grand decision, the heroic departure. But most beginnings are quieter. They happen when you decide to try one more time. When you choose to say the honest thing instead of the safe thing. When you write the first bad sentence. When you take the first uncertain step. When you let yourself hope again after promising yourself you wouldn’t.

Even now, in this small piece of writing, there is a beginning. I started with no plan except to follow whatever felt alive. And here we are, together, in this strange little clearing made of words.

If I could leave you with one thought, it would be this: pay attention to what quietly keeps you human. It might be music. It might be trees. It might be cooking, walking, reading, praying, drawing, listening to rain, holding a cup with both hands, watching an animal sleep, remembering a kindness, or simply allowing yourself to breathe without rushing toward the next task.

Whatever it is, don’t dismiss it. The world will tell you that only measurable things matter: productivity, achievement, status, speed. But the soul often speaks in smaller units. A pause. A glance. A line in a book. The smell of bread. The sound of someone calling your name.

Those are not minor things.

They are the places where life touches us and says, softly, “You are still here.”

And maybe that is enough for today. Maybe that is more than enough.
